title: A Hitchhiker's Guide to SAP Fiori UX in the Age of AI
author: OliverGraeff
text:
Don't Panic. The user experience of SAP is evolving fast, but there's still a clear map. And on November 24, 2026 , I'll walk you through it in one hour. 
 What This Is About 
 SAP Fiori remains the user experience foundation for SAP applications. But in 2026, the way users work with SAP solutions has fundamentally shifted. The same holds for the way developers build them. 
 Joule Work has emerged as the new UI for AI, becoming the primary engagement layer for business users. Joule Studio is the new AI-first development environment for creating agents, apps, and workflows. And familiar technologies like SAPUI5, SAP Fiori elements, and SAP Build haven't gone away, they've evolved and gained new roles in this landscape. 
 If you've ever caught yourself wondering: 
 How does SAP Fiori fit into a world where Joule is everywhere? 
 What's the relationship between Joule Work, Joule Studio, and SAP Build? 
 Where do I start or continue my learning journey in 2026? 
 …then this webinar is for you. 

 Who Should Join 
 This session is designed for everyone : executives, project managers, UX leads, key users, consultants, and developers alike. Whether you've been following SAP Fiori for years or are just now trying to take first steps, you'll leave with a clear mental map of how the pieces fit together today. 
 Agenda 
 This one-hour webinar is structured around the key layers of the SAP UX landscape: 

 SAP Fiori: The UX Foundation The design system, SAPUI5, SAP Fiori elements, and why they still matter in the age of AI. 

 Run: Where Users Meet SAP Apps SAP Build Work Zone, Joule Work as the new AI engagement layer, and the Joule Work mobile app. 

 Adapt: Extending Standard SAP Apps How key users and developers extend standard SAP apps with easy-to-use, AI-assisted tools in a Clean Core compliant way. 

 Develop: Building Applications in the Age of AI Joule Studio, SAP Build Code, ABAP development tools, and AI-powered development workflows. 

 Wrap-Up and Learning Resources Your entry points for hands-on learning, followed by a live Q&A. 
 Session Details 
 Date: Monday, November 24, 2026 
 Time: 16:00 – 17:00 CET 
 Watch on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/live/nZq6Z6ZlZnc 
 I have been presenting the Hitchhiker's Guide series since 2022 and update it annually to reflect the latest shifts in the SAP UX landscape. You can find recordings of previous editions on SAP Community, including last year's two-part series . If you attended a previous edition, this is worth your hour. A lot has happened. See you on November 24.

title: CAP Agents that collaborates with humans - Announcing `cap-agents-sdm-backend` plugin
author: merbinjanselm
text:
In my earlier articles, we explored how CAP agents can remember useful information across conversations and find relevant passages in documents using vector stores . But knowledge work often continues beyond finding an answer. 
 A project assistant or a manager may need to read last week's report, follow a reporting template, prepare this week's update, and save it where the team can review it. The result needs to become a document people can continue working with. 
 Enterprise Content Management has been a central piece in enterprises for document collaboration through role-based access control and audited work through versioning. 
 In this post, I'm introducing @mi8y/cap-agents-sdm-backend : an open-source add-on that lets CAP agents work on content and collaborate with humans via SAP Document Management or any compliant CMIS 1.1 repositories through an unified access layer. 
 SDM as a filesystem for knowledge work 
 With CAP v10 and the @cap-js/agents plugin , developers can build Calesi-pattern agents within CAP applications. CAP provides the application framework, while the underlying agent harness coordinates the model and its tools. 
 Tools such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex offer a useful illustration of this working style. An agent explores folders, reads instructions, finds relevant files, and saves its work. The filesystem gives it a practical way to organise and revisit content. 
 That pattern is useful for business content too. Imagine a workspace containing the following folder layout: 
 File content layout for agentic work 
 The agent can read the instructions ( AGENTS.md ), discover how to prepare a report (via Agent Skills), inspect earlier work (previously created files), and write a new document. With this backend, the content lives in SAP Document Management rather than on the application's local disk, accessed as a virtual filesystem. 
 These file operations do not require a shell or a code-execution tool. Hence, this is a better and a more secured approach. The backend translates them into requests to the document repository via the CMIS 1.1 protocol . 
 A filesystem view for the agent, with content stored in SAP Document Management 
 @mi8y/cap-agents-sdm-backend implements the Deep Agents filesystem backend interface for SAP Document Management via CMIS Browser Binding . It is designed to be used with CAP Node.js 10 or later. 
 It gives the agent familiar operations to: 
 Browse folders and read files ( ls command) 
 Create files, including missing parent folders below its configured workspace. ( mkdir and >> operations) 
 Edit text within existing files ( >> operation) 
 Find files by path patterns and search for literal text in their contents ( grep command) 
 This is direct file access. This is in stark contrast to Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) through 'Semantic retrieval' using a vector store. 
 The CMIS Browser Binding approach also makes compatible CMIS repositories a possible backing store or virtual filesystem, subject to their supported capabilities and connection setup. 
 The source code is open-source and MIT licensed. 
 A shared workspace for people and agent collaboration 
 The most useful part is that the documents remain available with people too. 
 An agent can prepare a report, a team member (human) can review and revise it, and a later conversation can use the saved report as its starting point. The document becomes a shared work product that remains useful beyond the chat. 
 Content Management Interoperability Services v1.1 (CMIS) brings the content-management layer. Depending on the repository and configuration, this includes role-based access and document or folder permissions, version history, and the auditing capabilities. SAP's Document Management has in-built access controls and versioning for supported repositories. 
 Collaboration here means people and agents contributing to content in the same repository, through their respective interfaces i.e. UI for humans, while filesystem interface for agents. 
 People and agents collaborate together on documents 
 Example: Project Reporting Assistant 
 I added a basic reports assistant example in the repository demonstrating this pattern in a CAP application with an embedded SAPUI5 Document Management ReuseUI and an agent chat. 
 The workspace contains agent instructions, reporting skills, and templates. A user supplies a few updates: Create this week's project status report for Northstar.

Integration testing is complete.
Environment access is still pending.
Carry forward the open actions from the previous report. 
 The agent reads the relevant instructions and template, consults the previous report, and saves a new text report in the repository. The user can then open the output report for review. 
 The example includes project status reports, incident reports, and executive briefings. For instance, an incident report can become the source for a later leadership briefing. 
 In the demo, instructions ( AGENTS.md ) and skills (Agent Skills) also live in SAP Document Management. Teams can update that content in the repository and start a new chat to load the revised instructions. 
 Team begins a conversation with an agent, and collaborates on the content 
 Demo of Project Reporting Assistant 
 Getting started 
 Install the package in your CAP agent application: npm install @mi8y/cap-agents-sdm-backend 
 The SdmBackend backend can automatically use the service-binding flow if having an SDM instance binding or can use a configured Cloud SDK destination. And the configured root folder lets the application expose a selected part of the repository as the agent's workspace. 
 There is no additional CDS persistence model or cds add step for document storage. The package README explains configuration, and the complete example shows the CAP integration and document UI. 
 Start with text-based content such as instructions, templates, and reports. Access to a file does not automatically provide native editing of Word documents, spreadsheets, or PDFs. Likewise, prompt instructions asking for confirmation or protecting templates need enforceable application controls when those are business requirements. 
 With this add-on, a CAP agent can leave behind more than a chat response: a report, a working draft, or an updated document that the team can pick up and continue. 
 Try the example, adapt the workspace to your use case, and share feedback or issues in the repository .

title: Personnel Calculation Rule - Factoring Parameter
author: Rithika_M21
text:
Introduction 
 Accurate payroll execution is the backbone of employee life cycle management, and ensuring employees are compensated precisely for days worked—while factoring in complex absence structures—is a critical daily challenge for SAP consultants. In this blog post, we will walk through a practical Personnel Calculation Rule (PCR) that bridges Time Management and Payroll by leveraging variables like TKSOLL and TKAP to determine exact calendar days worked and streamline wage type valuation. 
 Importance of PCR: 
 In an employee life cycle payroll plays a major role. Generally an employee gets paid for the number of days worked in a particular payroll period/cycle. Payroll calculations takes place based company policy. Here let's take a scenario where they excludes paid absence and finds exact calendar days an employee worked in a particular period 
 Operations used: 
 TKSOLL - Takes planned working time in Calendar days. 
 TKAP** - Paid absence in Calendar days. 
 PCR Syntax: 
 * 
 XXXX 
 RTE=TKSOLL * Sets rate to planned calendar days 
 RTE-TKAP** * Subtracts unpaid absences 
 ADDWT * * Adds wage type to output table 
 PCR Image: 

 Explanation: 
 In the above sample PCR we initially check for the wagetype which needs to be processed. 
 Then we set Rate equals to TKSOLL, which means the rate is equal to number of calendar days in planned working time. This varies from employee to employee based on the work schedule which is assigned to them. The work schedule determines the working time/shift of an employee with breaks, public holidays configured in it. 
 Then the rate is being subtracted by the paid absence with counting class 06 followed by paid absence with counting class 07 and 09. 
 Finally stores the calculated Rate in the wage type which is being processed. 
 Conclusion: 
 Mastering payroll factoring through custom PCRs gives you the flexibility to meet organizational policies by utilizing TKSOLL for planned calendar days and subtracting paid absences via TKAP to reflect true working times. Implementing this approach improves accuracy and transparency across your payroll and time management modules, so feel free to share your thoughts, questions, or alternative approaches in the comments below.

title: ONB 2.0: Recruiter-Based Task Assignment
author: AtakanBozkurt
text:
SAP SuccessFactors Onboarding 2.0: Assigning the Recruiter from Recruiting as the Responsible User for Review New Hire Data and Onboarding Tasks 
 A business requirement that SAP does not support through its standard direct assignment scenario was addressed with a custom solution combining existing configuration components. In this article, I describe the implementation that assigns the Recruiter specified on the Job Requisition in Recruiting as the responsible user for both the Review New Hire Data step and Onboarding tasks. 
 SAP KBA 3550964 (Mapping roles in the JobRelType to New Hire Data Review Step assignee) and KBA 3599479 (Is it possible to delegate New Hire Data Review Task to someone else?) are the references we consulted regarding standard product behavior in this area. The method described here is not a standard feature published by SAP; it is a custom configuration developed as part of a project and must be validated in the relevant environment. 
 Important prerequisite: This solution relies on resolving the Employee HR role through the HR Manager relationship in Job Relationships. If the HR Manager relationship is used to represent a different person in the organization, this design may alter the existing relationship, route tasks to the wrong person, and may not be suitable. Check the existing use of Job Relationships before implementation. 
 The method consists of two parallel assignment paths: For Review New Hire Data, the Recruiter information is transferred to a custom employmentInfo field, and the responsible group is determined through ONB2ResponsibilityConfig. For other Onboarding tasks, an HR Manager relationship is created through Job Relationships mapping; the Employee HR role in the general HRBP Responsible Group resolves the relevant user based on that relationship. 
 Job Requisition Field and Save Rule 
 First, create a custom picklist field for Job Relationship Type in the Job Requisition Template. Its ID can be custJobRelType. This field must use the standard jobRelType picklist. Verify that Manage Business Configuration → Job Relationship → Job Relationship Type is configured with the same picklist. Since the field is used for background mapping, it does not have to be visible to end users. 
 <field-definition id="custJobRelType" type="picklist" required="false" custom="true">
 <field-label><![CDATA[Job Relationship Type]]></field-label>
 <field-label lang="en_US"><![CDATA[Job Relationship Type]]></field-label>
 <field-description><![CDATA[]]></field-description>
 <picklist-id>jobRelType</picklist-id>
</field-definition> 
 XML: custJobRelType field definition for the Job Requisition Template 
 In Admin Center → Manage Rules in Recruiting, open the Job Requisition tab and select the template in use. Then, under Configure Business Rules, create a rule using the “Configure Business Rules on Job Requisition” scenario with Purpose = Save. IF = Always True; THEN = Job Requisition Template.Job Relationship Type = HR Manager. 

 Manage Rules in Recruiting: selecting an active Job Requisition Template 

 Save Rule: setting Job Relationship Type to HR Manager 
 Assign the rule to the Save section of all relevant Job Requisition Templates in use. This automatically populates the relationship type when the requisition is saved. 
 Recruit-to-Hire Data Mapping for Job Relationships 
 In Admin Center → Recruit-to-Hire Data Mapping → Job Relationships, create new mapping rows. In the implemented design, Relationship Type is sourced from the custom Job Relationship Type field on the Job Requisition; the related user is sourced from Recruiter (recruiterName); and the relationship start date is sourced from Start Date. Check the corresponding technical fields for these three mappings in your own template. 

 Recruit-to-Hire Data Mapping: Job Relationships mappings 
 Employment Information Field and Review New Hire Data Assignment 
 Under Admin Center → Manage Business Configuration → employmentInfo, configure an available custom String field. The example below uses custom-string24; a different custom string field can also be selected. 

 Manage Business Configuration: employmentInfo object 
 Field settings: 
 Identifier = custom-string24; 
 Label = HRBP (ONB); 
 Enabled = Yes; 
 Mandatory = No; 
 Data Type = STRING; 
 Type of Reference Object = Foundation Object; 
 Reference Object = ONB2ResponsibilityConfig; 
 Maximum Length = 256. 
 As this field is intended for background use, it does not need to be displayed on the candidate screen. 
 Next, under Recruit-to-Hire Data Mapping → Employment Information (employmentInfo), map custom-string24 to the source Job Requisition Template → Recruiter (recruiterName). This transfers the Recruiter information to the field used by the Review New Hire Data responsibility rule. 

 Employment Information: mapping custom-string24 to Recruiter 
 In Configure Business Rules, configure the SFCC_ResponsibleForNewHireDataReview rule using the “Assign Responsibility Group for New Hire Data Review” scenario. The rule selects the relevant Responsible Group from the employmentInfo field referencing ONB2ResponsibilityConfig. The Responsible Group ID created for each Recruiter must match the technical value resolved from this field. Verify the exact IF/THEN expression against the environment configuration shown in the screenshot below. 

 SFCC_ResponsibleForNewHireDataReview: rule determining the Responsible Group 
 Responsible Groups: 
 In Admin Center → Onboarding General Settings → Manage Responsible Groups, first create the general HRBP group. ID = HRBP, Group Name = HRBP, Roles = Employee HR. Leave Users and Dynamic Groups empty. This general group will be assigned to Onboarding tasks in the program. 

 General HRBP Responsible Group: Employee HR role 
 On the same screen, create a separate, user-specific Responsible Group for each Recruiter/HRBP. The Group ID and name must match the relevant employee ID; add only the corresponding employee to Users; leave Roles and Dynamic Groups empty. The value 642317 in the example is illustrative. These are the groups identified by the Review New Hire Data rule. 

 User-specific Responsible Group: employee ID and user 
 This distinction is critical: Review New Hire Data identifies the user-specific group ID through the custom field and rule. Other tasks in the Onboarding program are assigned to the general HRBP group; the Employee HR role in this group resolves to the user designated as HR Manager through Job Relationships mapping. 
 Task Assignment in the Onboarding Program 
 In Admin Center → Manage Onboarding and Offboarding Programs, open the relevant program. Edit the task to be routed under Primary New Hire Tasks or Secondary New Hire Tasks. Select Task Attributes → Assigned to = HRBP. The same setting was used for the Equipment task, for example. Repeat this assignment for other relevant tasks. 

 Onboarding Program: Task Attributes → Assigned to = HRBP 
 Conclusion and Considerations 
 In this custom solution, the Recruiter information serves two separate mechanisms. For Review New Hire Data, a user-specific group is selected using an ONB2ResponsibilityConfig Lookup. For Onboarding tasks, an HR Manager relationship is created through Job Relationships, and the assignment is made to the general HRBP group using the Employee HR role. Thus, instead of a direct Recruiter → Task Assignee mapping, existing responsibility and relationship mechanisms are combined. 
 Before go-live, test each candidate to confirm that the Recruiter user ID resolves correctly, the Job Relationship is created with the correct person and start date, the user-specific Responsible Group ID matches its value, and both task types are assigned to the correct user. If the HR Manager relationship is used in other processes, this method should not be implemented, or the design should be reassessed. 
 Note: If dashboard visibility is separated based on Granted Users / Target Population permissions after this structure is configured, each Recruiter will see only their own candidates on the dashboard. However, because the configuration steps for this adjustment are not included in the document, this blog technically explains only the task assignee solution; it does not cover the separation of dashboard visibility.

title: SAP Business Network for Logistics 2610 – What’s New?
author: CorinnaKramer
text:
The October 2026 release of SAP Business Network for Logistics brings a focused set of enhancements across both SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration and SAP Business Network Global Track and Trace. This post walks through the highlights — what's new, what it means for you, and where to find more detail. 

 Cross SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration and SAP Business Network Global Track and Trace 
 Feature enhancement for integration logs 
 The 'Manage Integration Log' app has been upgraded. You can switch to it by clicking the 'New Version' button in the upper right corner of the app. 

 The old version is deprecated with this release but remains available alongside the new one for several months, giving you time to make the transition at your own pace. The end-of-life date for the old version will be communicated once confirmed. 
 What's new in the app: 
 Improved search: new header search fields for ‘Document ID’, ‘Type Description’, ‘Scenario’, and ‘Correlation ID’ make it faster to find specific entries in high-volume environments. 
 Richer filtering: the header now includes ‘Overall Status’ and ‘Business Partner’ filters alongside the existing ‘Document ID’ and ‘Received On’ filters. 
 Built-in Analytics: a new ‘Analytics’ tab shows the volume and status of application message types — such as ‘TransportationOrderRequest’ for Freight Collaboration or ‘TrackedProcessAndEvent’ for Global Track and Trace — giving you an at-a-glance operational picture. 

 Expanded exports: higher export limits reduce manual filtering and support complete dataset retrieval for audit, compliance, and operational reporting. 
 Clearer error handling: when you select multiple messages for reprocessing, error messages are now displayed individually per correlation ID in a more readable format — making troubleshooting significantly easier. 
 Why it matters: integration logs are central to managing the health of your network connections. The new analytics capability in particular turns the app from a reactive troubleshooting tool into a proactive monitoring dashboard. Higher export limits are especially valuable for customers running high transaction volumes who need complete datasets for compliance reporting. 
 2027 Release Schedule Now Available 
 The release schedule for 2027 is now published for both SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration and SAP Business Network Global Track and Trace. Planning ahead for system maintenance windows just got easier. 

 SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration 
 Action Required: Migrate to SAP Data Privacy Integration Next Generation Service 
 This one requires your attention. SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration is migrating from the Personal Data Manager to the Next Generation Data Privacy Integration service ahead of schedule (now October 17, 2026), requiring shippers to subscribe to the ngdpi plan and carriers to use the new Manage Personal Data app via a dedicated URL. 
 For shippers: 
 In your SAP Cloud Platform subaccount, subscribe to the Data Privacy Integration Next Generation service (application plan name: `ngdpi`). 
 Assign the `DPI_NextGen_Information_DataPrivacy_Administrator` role collection to users responsible for personal data management. 
 For full documentation, refer to Personal Data Record SAP Data Privacy Integration Next Generation Service on the SAP Help Portal. 
 For carriers: 
 You can use the ‘Manage Personal Data’ app of the Data Privacy Integration Next Generation service. The app is accessible at: 
 https://<your-subdomain>.app.<region(eu10/us20/us30)>.ngdpi.dpp.cloud.sap. 
 For more information, see Personal Data Record in the SAP Help Portal. 
 Why it matters: Staying on the current DPI service means relying on a deprecated integration path. Migrating to ngDPI ensures continued compliance with data privacy regulations and access to the latest capabilities for managing personal data records across your network. 

 Planning and Subcontracting Process Enhanced 
 This release brings several improvements to the freight subcontracting process, spanning API and EDI capabilities. 
 Product ID sharing via the Consumer API: 
 The ‘Consumer API for Freight Subcontracting’ now supports sharing the ‘Product ID’ with the carrier. This closes an information gap that previously required manual workarounds, enabling carriers to better plan and execute shipments for products requiring specific handling. 
 Richer date/time fields in the Provider API: 
 The ‘Provider API for Freight Subcontracting’ now exposes pickup start/end date and time as well as delivery start/end date and time as new fields. This gives carriers and logistics partners a much more precise picture of the time constraints associated with each leg of a subcontracted shipment — reducing misalignments and improving execution accuracy. 
 Star-shaped stage sequences in outsourced planning: 
 Outsourced planning for freight units now supports star-shaped and reverse star-shaped stage sequences — a common freight network topology where shipments converge to a hub before being distributed, or vice versa. 
 Notes and instructions via EDI 204: 
 It is now possible to share notes and instructions with carriers via EDI 204 using a new NTE node, supporting up to 20 segments. This expands the capacity to include additional notes or instructions in shipment EDI messages, which is useful for carriers and shippers exchanging richer data in complex multi-stop payloads 
 Why it matters: These enhancements collectively reduce friction in the subcontracting process. More data flowing between shippers and carriers via both API and EDI means fewer manual touchpoints, less room for misinterpretation, and ultimately better on-time performance. 
 Improved Booking Accuracy in Dock Appointment Scheduling 
 The ‘Manage Dock Appointments’ and ‘Self-Book Dock Appointments’ apps now display the ‘Location Description’ alongside the ‘Loading Point ID’ in edit mode, helping you make more accurate booking selections. 
 The location description is shown only when a location has been assigned to the loading point and a description was available at the time of the assignment. 
 Why it matters: A location description sounds like a small addition, but in practice it makes a real difference when multiple dock locations or warehouse areas share similar names. Displaying the description directly in booking details gives carriers and warehouse staff the context they need to arrive at the right location — reducing delays and misrouted arrivals. 

 SAP Business Network Global Track and Trace 
 Standard Extractor Enhancements: More Data Flowing from SAP S/4HANA 
 Three new data points are now transferred from SAP Transportation Management in SAP S/4HANA to SAP Business Network Global Track and Trace via the standard extractor: 
 Administrative audit data: ‘Created By/On’ and ‘Changed By/On’ fields are now included in the data transferred to GTT. This supports traceability and audit requirements by making it clear when a freight order or booking was created and who made changes — directly within the GTT visibility layer. 
 Container details: ‘Container ID’ and ‘Container type’ can now be sent to GTT via the container table. This information can be used for visibility providers to calculate carbon emissions. By default, the feature is disabled. You can enable it manually. For more information, see Send Containers Table to the GTT System . 
 Ordering party: The ‘Ordering Party’ for freight orders and bookings is now transferred to GTT. This supports more accurate downstream reporting and visibility, especially in complex multi-party logistics scenarios where the ordering party differs from the shipper. 
 For more information, see 3763702 
 Why it matters: Better data in GTT means better visibility. Audit data supports compliance; container details unlock more accurate sustainability metrics; and the ordering party field closes an attribution gap in multi-party logistics flows. These are steady improvements to data completeness that pay dividends across reporting, compliance, and operational monitoring. 
 Improved Shipment Visibility: EDI 214 Carrier Tracking Numbers Now Visible 
 Carrier tracking numbers sent by carriers via EDI 214 (L11 segment) are now automatically visible in SAP Business Network Global Track and Trace. 
 A new mapping was added between two data points: 
 EDI side: The L11 segment with qualifier CI (Unique Consignment Identifier) — this is where carriers include their tracking number in an EDI message 
 API side: The carrierDocumentReference field in the POST /OrderEvents API — this is how GTT (Global Track and Trace) receives that tracking number 
 Why it matters: Previously, if a carrier sent a tracking number via EDI, it would not be passed through to GTT. Now it is — meaning the tracking number travels end-to-end from the carrier's EDI message all the way into SAP Business Network Global Track and Trace, giving shippers and logistics teams better shipment visibility without needing to look up tracking numbers elsewhere. 

 What's Coming Next: Join Our 2611 Webcast

title: S/4HANA Cloud Public–Cost deferral (EBRR) on non-billable service order items linked to a contract
author: Iri_pr
text:
Hello experts, 
 we are implementing SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition (Service Order Management 3D2, Service Contract Management 3MO, Event-Based Revenue Recognition – Service Documents 3M3). We are trying to solve a cost deferral requirement and would appreciate any advice or experience. 
 Business context 
 Our customer performs cyclic and extraordinary maintenance on machines. 
 Billing is done from the service contract using an ad-hoc billing plan, typically a down payment (e.g. 75%) when work is completed, and the final invoice in the following quarter. 
 Service orders are used only to collect costs: stock materials issued (service part items), purchased materials/services, and internal labor hours coming from an external system. The service order items are not billable and the service orders reference the service contract. 
 Requirement 
 Costs posted on the service orders must not be recognized immediately . They must be deferred and recognized only at final billing, together with the related revenue. In other words, we need costs and revenue to be matched: costs on the service order, revenue on the referenced contract. 
 What we observe in the standard 
 Non-billable service order items: costs are recognized immediately. We set the recognition key CCOCC (Completed Contract – Service Order) manually on the non-billable item in the app Revenue Recognition (Event-Based) – Service Documents before the goods issue. The goods issue cost was still recognized immediately (no COS adjustment, no Deferred COS). 
 Key derivation: in the SSCUI Derivation of Recognition Key for Service Documents (102968) we cannot enter the non-billable item category. It seems only billing-relevant item categories are allowed. 
 Billable item with zero value (workaround): if we add a billable item with value 0 and CCOCC, the deferral works as expected: Actual Cost 135, COS Adjustment –135, Deferred COS 135. However: 
 the job Schedule Technical Completion for Financial Close does not set TECO, with the warning: “Invoices must be created for the item and posted to financial accounting. Status of the account assignment object stays Released.” 
 this item will never be invoiced (billing is done from the contract), so the costs would remain deferred indefinitely; 
 creating a zero-value invoice just to reach TECO is not acceptable for fiscal reasons (Italian e-invoicing / SdI, tax postings, fiscal numbering). 
 Financial hierarchy with service contract as root item: this seems to be exactly the intended solution, since service order costs are collected on the contract item where revenue is. However, as far as we understand it requires a dedicated contract item category with the flag “Root Item in Financial Hierarchy” . We cannot create new item categories in our Public Cloud tenant, and we are not sure whether the scenario is available in Public Cloud at all. 
 Questions 
 Is there a standard way in S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition to defer costs on non-billable service order items referencing a billable service contract, and recognize them when the contract is billed? 
 Is the financial hierarchy with service contract item as root item available in Public Cloud? If so, is there an SAP-delivered contract item category with the root flag, or another way to activate it? 
 If we keep a billable item that will never be invoiced , is there any standard way to set TECO on it (e.g. a billing status, rejection reason or other setting) so that EBRR releases the deferred costs at period-end closing, without issuing an invoice? 
 Has anyone faced a similar scenario (contract billing + service order cost collection + cost deferral) in Public Cloud, and how did you solve it? 
 Thank you in advance for any input!

My understanding is that this may be due to the relevant counters being reinitialized during the truncation process, effectively resetting the OAM page count to zero.  Could someone with in-depth knowledge of ASE internals clarify this point? title: #Demystifying AI Series — Ep 4: # "SAP BTP's AI Foundation — The Engine Room Nobody Shows You"
author: Benjelloun_Mhammed
text:
DEMYSTIFYING AI SERIES · EPISODE 04 
 "SAP BTP's AI Foundation — The Engine Room Nobody Shows You" 

 💡 Every time Joule answers a question or runs a task, something invisible makes it possible. SAP calls it AI Foundation. Nobody talks about it — but it's the reason enterprise AI at SAP actually works, and the reason your job will change in ways you can't see yet. 

 The Room Behind the Stage 
 You've been to a theater. 
 The performance is up front — lights, actors, dialogue. It all looks seamless. But somewhere backstage there's a generator, a lighting rig, a sound system, crew members running cue sheets. Without all of that, there is no performance. 
 Joule is the performance. 
 SAP BTP's AI Foundation is the room behind the stage. 
 When Joule answers your question about an overdue purchase order, or an agent autonomously routes an approval workflow, or the system summarizes a supplier contract in seconds — none of that happens because of Joule alone. It happens because AI Foundation is running underneath it, managing the models, routing the requests, governing the data access, logging every decision. 
 Most people never see it. That's by design. But if you work in the SAP ecosystem — as a consultant, an architect, a functional expert — understanding what's back there will change how you think about everything SAP is building. 
 What Is SAP AI Foundation? 
 SAP positions AI Foundation as the "operating system for AI" on BTP. 
 That framing is intentional. Just as an operating system abstracts the hardware from the application, AI Foundation abstracts the complexity of AI infrastructure from the teams building on top of it. You don't need to manage GPU clusters, handle model versioning, or wire up security frameworks from scratch. The platform does it. 
 At its core, AI Foundation is a set of services that run on SAP BTP — services that Joule, SAP's business applications, and custom extensions all use to do anything AI-related. 
 It covers three things your organization needs before AI can actually work at enterprise scale: 
 Access to models — a governed, unified way to use large language models without every team reinventing authentication, rate limiting, and cost tracking from scratch. 
 Infrastructure to run AI workloads — a managed runtime that handles the scaling, deployment, and lifecycle of AI models and agents in a secure, compliant environment. 
 A governance layer — the audit trails, access controls, metering, and monitoring that enterprise customers require before they'll let AI anywhere near regulated processes. 
 Without these three, AI in an enterprise isn't a product. It's a prototype. 
 The Key Components 
 Let me walk through what's actually inside AI Foundation — in plain terms, not product documentation. 
 SAP AI Core — The Runtime Engine 
 Think of AI Core as the power plant. 
 It's the managed execution environment where AI workloads actually run. When you deploy an AI model, when Joule executes a skill, when a custom extension calls a language model — AI Core handles the underlying compute. It manages scaling, model lifecycle, and deployment pipelines. 
 Developers and architects care about AI Core when they're building or deploying AI-powered applications. Business users almost never interact with it directly — but every AI capability they use runs through it. 
 Generative AI Hub — The Model Switchboard 
 Here's a practical problem: different AI use cases need different models. A model that's great at summarizing legal contracts might not be the best for coding assistance or customer sentiment analysis. And the best model today might be replaced by a better one in six months. 
 Generative AI Hub solves this by providing a single, unified API to multiple large language models — from SAP, from third-party providers, and from the open-source ecosystem. Teams build against one consistent interface, and the hub handles which model gets called, how, and under what constraints. 
 It also provides orchestration capabilities: prompt management, reusable prompt templates, content moderation, and grounding integrations. This is where the SAP HANA Cloud Vector Engine plugs in — documents and business data can be embedded and retrieved to ground AI responses in your actual business context, not just general model knowledge. 
 For anyone building custom AI capabilities on BTP, the Generative AI Hub is where most of the interesting work happens. 
 SAP AI Launchpad — The Operations Panel 
 AI Core and the Generative AI Hub are developer and platform tools. AI Launchpad is what the humans running AI in production use to manage what's deployed, monitor what's running, and experiment with what's possible. 
 It provides a UI for model lifecycle management, deployment oversight, and experimentation — including a prompt editor and chat interface for testing models before they go into production flows. 
 Think of it as the cockpit for the AI runtime. 
 Joule Studio — Where Business AI Gets Built 
 Joule Studio is the newest and most visible piece of the AI Foundation picture. 
 It's the low-code, business-facing environment where organizations can build custom Joule skills and AI agents — without writing platform infrastructure code. An HR team can build a skill that drafts offer letters from a role profile. A procurement team can build an agent that tracks supplier risk across open orders. 
 These capabilities are built on top of AI Foundation — they use AI Core to run, they call models through the Generative AI Hub, they ground answers through the Vector Engine. Joule Studio abstracts all of that behind a composable, business-oriented interface. 
 This is where SAP's vision of "thousands of AI agents across the enterprise" becomes buildable by people who understand the business process, not just the platform. 
 How It Connects to What You Already Know 
 Here's the picture assembled. 
 S/4HANA, SuccessFactors, Ariba — your business applications. When Joule runs inside them, it's calling AI Foundation services to fulfil your request. 
 HANA Cloud — provides the data storage and the Vector and Graph engines that enable grounding. When you AI Agent gives you an answer specific to your business, HANA Cloud's Vector Engine retrieved the relevant context. 
 AI Core — runs the models. Generative AI Hub routes the model calls. AI Launchpad monitors it all. 
 Joule Studio — where your organisation can extend all of this with custom skills and agents, without rebuilding the infrastructure layer. 
 And sitting under all of it, handling security, compliance, access control, and audit: the governance layer that makes it defensible to your legal team and your auditors. 
 Why This Matters Even If You Never Touch It 
 Here's the honest answer to the question in every prior episode: why should I care about this? 
 Most SAP professionals will never write a line of code for AI Core. Most will never configure a Generative AI Hub deployment. That's fine. 
 But here's what you will do: 
 Advise clients on whether to adopt AI capabilities. 
 Scope projects that include Joule-powered workflows. 
 Evaluate whether an SAP AI feature is ready for production in a regulated environment. 
 Explain to a steering committee why their SAP investment now includes an "AI Foundation" they've never heard of. 
 Understanding what's in the engine room doesn't make you a mechanic. It makes you the person in the room who knows why the lights are on — and what it takes to keep them on. 
 That's not a niche skill. That's the work. 

 Your Turn 
 In your current SAP landscape — whether it's a customer project, your own organisation, or a system you support — where do you see the first realistic use case for a custom Joule skill or agent? Not theoretical. Something someone is already doing manually that takes longer than it should. 

 That's probably where AI Foundation will show up first. 

 Drop your answer in the comments. I'm curious whether the gap is in the process, the data, or the organisational readiness to trust the output. 
 ⏭ Next episode: HANA Cloud's Vector and Graph engines — what they actually do, and why they're the difference between AI that knows your business and AI that just sounds like it does.

title: CDS View Performance Best Practice – UNION in a LEFT OUTER JOIN
author: HermannGahm
text:
UNION in a LEFT OUTER JOIN - CDS (SQL) performance anti-pattern 
 This blog post focuses on the CDS view performance anti-pattern called "UNION in LEFT OUTER JOIN" and it's part of the CDS View Performance Best Practices series. You can find an introduction to CDS View performance recommendations, aspects you need to consider in terms of performance, and a list of all available CDS anti-patterns in the following blog post: 
 CDS View Performance Best Practices 

 Why this pattern deserves attention 
 A UNION in the right-hand input of a LEFT OUTER JOIN is logically valid. The risk is performance: on large data volumes and complex data models, both UNION branches may be processed before a selective filter from the left side of the join can reduce them. In simple and highly selective cases, the optimizer may apply semi-join reduction. In more complex plans, that optimization is not guaranteed because plan selection is cost based. 

 The business example 
 A retail company tracks customer orders for multiple sales regions. Each order is fulfilled through one of two independent delivery systems: a central warehouse or a regional warehouse. Fulfillment is exclusive in this model: an order is only assigned to one delivery system. Some orders are still open and therefore have no delivery record. The data below is intentionally minimal so that result of every row can be easily followed through each query variant by hand. 
 Data model 
 The following three tables are created and populated by the complete runnable SQL at the end of this post. All rows are shown so every query result can be verified by hand. 
 Table: ORDERS 

 ORDER_ID 
 REGION_ID 

 ORD100 
 1 

 ORD200 
 1 

 ORD300 
 2 

 ORD400 
 2 

 ORD500 
 2 
 ORD400 is still open and has no delivery in either system and therefore is not part of the following tables. 
 Table: CENTRAL_DELIVERIES 

 ORDER_ID 
 DELIVERY_DATE 

 ORD100 
 2026-09-10 

 ORD300 
 2026-09-15 

 ORD900 
 2026-08-20 
 ORD900 is an older, delivered order that is not part of the current ORDERS selection. 
 Table: REGIONAL_DELIVERIES 

 ORDER_ID 
 DELIVERY_DATE 

 ORD200 
 2026-09-12 

 ORD500 
 2026-09-18 

 ORD950 
 2026-08-25 
 ORD950 is another older, delivered order that is not part of the current ORDERS selection. 

 The original, correct query 
 The query goal is to list every order together with its delivery date from Region 2 (region_id = 2), regardless of which delivery system handled it. Open orders must still appear with a NULL delivery date — the LEFT OUTER JOIN is the mechanism that guarantees this. with deliveries as (
 select order_id, delivery_date
 from central_deliveries
 union all
 select order_id, delivery_date
 from regional_deliveries
)
select o.order_id,
 o.region_id,
 d.delivery_date
 from orders o
 left outer join deliveries d
 on o.order_id = d.order_id
 where o.region_id = 2; 
 Please note that the query uses a common table expression (CTE). T he with_clause creates a temporary result set based on its subquery. The native SQL approach uses the WITH clause for simplicity, avoiding multiple view definitions and lengthy code snippets while showing the essence of the anti-pattern in a single executable statement. 
 Technically, this has the same effect as when a CDS view uses an association (technically a LEFT OUTER JOIN) to another CDS view that contains a UNION. 
 The main query selects from the table ORDERS and uses the temporary view (CTE) DELIVERIES in a LEFT OUTER JOIN. The CTE DELIVERIES contains a UNION ALL of the two delivery tables CENTRAL_DELIVERIES and REGIONAL_DELIVERIES. 
 Correct and expected result of the query: 

 ORDER_ID 
 REGION_ID 
 DELIVERY_DATE 

 ORD300 
 2 
 2026-09-15 

 ORD400 
 2 
 NULL 

 ORD500 
 2 
 2026-09-18 

 Let’s look at the execution plan for the query. 

 The plan places the UNION ALL below the LEFT OUTER JOIN, this means the UNION ALL is executed before the LEFT OUTER JOIN. The filtered ORDERS table is the left input, while CENTRAL_DELIVERIES and REGIONAL_DELIVERIES are combined as the right input. 
 The UNION ALL combines the rows from both delivery tables so that an order can match a delivery stored in either table. The LEFT OUTER JOIN then keeps every selected Region 2 order, including ORD400, for which neither table contains a delivery record. 
 The plan does not show the selected order IDs being used to reduce the scans of CENTRAL_DELIVERIES and REGIONAL_DELIVERIES. Rows that cannot match a selected order are therefore processed. 
 Can the filtered ORDERS input and the LEFT OUTER JOIN be pushed into the individual UNION ALL branches to reduce the data earlier? 

 The tempting but incorrect rewrite 
 At first glance, it may seem attractive to push the filtered ORDERS input and the LEFT OUTER JOIN into each UNION ALL branch: with deliveries_wrong_opt as (
 select o.order_id, o.region_id,
 cd.delivery_date
 from orders o
 left outer join central_deliveries cd
 on o.order_id = cd.order_id
 where o.region_id = 2
 union all
 select o.order_id, o.region_id,
 rd.delivery_date
 from orders o
 left outer join regional_deliveries rd
 on o.order_id = rd.order_id
 where o.region_id = 2
)
select * from deliveries_wrong_opt; 
 Why it fails: Each LEFT OUTER JOIN independently preserves every selected order. ORD300 has a matching row in CENTRAL_DELIVERIES, but not in REGIONAL_DELIVERIES therefore the regional branch produces a NULL-extended row for it. ORD500 has the symmetric problem. ORD400 has no match in either delivery table, so both branches produce a NULL-extended row for it. 
 The UNION ALL then combines the independently produced branch results. Consequently, the rewritten query returns six rows instead of the expected three. The additional rows are not caused by UNION ALL itself; they arise because each LEFT OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched orders independently. 

 ORDER_ID 
 REGION_ID 
 DELIVERY_DATE 

 ORD300 
 2 
 2026-09-15 

 ORD300 
 2 
 NULL 

 ORD400 
 2 
 NULL 

 ORD400 
 2 
 NULL 

 ORD500 
 2 
 NULL 

 ORD500 
 2 
 2026-09-18 
 The execution plan shows both the performance appeal and the structural problem of this rewrite: 

 The UNION ALL is now above two separate LEFT OUTER JOIN operators. Each branch reads the filtered Region 2 rows from ORDERS and joins them independently with one delivery table: the first branch with CENTRAL_DELIVERIES and the second with REGIONAL_DELIVERIES. Because only the selected orders participate in each join, fewer rows may be passed from the join branches into the UNION ALL. 
 The earlier reduction therefore looks attractive from a performance perspective, but it changes the result. Because both joins are LEFT OUTER JOINs, each branch preserves all three Region 2 orders before the branch results are combined. A match in one branch does not prevent the other branch from producing a NULL-extended row for the same order. For this data set, the UNION ALL consequently receives three rows from each branch and returns the six rows shown above. 
 If the LEFT OUTER JOIN cannot be pushed down into the UNION ALL branches, can the delivery tables still be reduced earlier without changing the result? 

 A semantics-preserving manual reduction 
 The LEFT OUTER JOIN cannot safely be pushed down into the UNION ALL branches. Therefore, we describe an approach where the selected order IDs can be used to reduce each delivery table before the tables are combined. 
 The query first creates selected_order_keys, containing the order IDs for Region 2. Each delivery table is then joined with these IDs, so only deliveries for the selected orders enter the UNION ALL. The LEFT OUTER JOIN remains in the main query and therefore still returns open orders, such as ORD400, exactly once. with selected_order_keys as (
 select distinct order_id
 from orders
 where region_id = 2
),
reduced_deliveries as (
 select d.order_id, d.delivery_date
 from central_deliveries d
 inner join selected_order_keys k
 on k.order_id = d.order_id
 union all
 select d.order_id, d.delivery_date
 from regional_deliveries d
 inner join selected_order_keys k
 on k.order_id = d.order_id
)
select o.order_id,
 o.region_id,
 d.delivery_date
 from orders o
 left outer join reduced_deliveries d
 on d.order_id = o.order_id
 where o.region_id = 2; 
 The DISTINCT ensures that each order ID occurs only once in selected_order_keys. Otherwise, duplicate IDs could multiply matching rows in the delivery tables. 
 This query produces the correct and expected result: 

 ORDER_ID 
 REGION_ID 
 DELIVERY_DATE 

 ORD300 
 2 
 2026-09-15 

 ORD400 
 2 
 NULL 

 ORD500 
 2 
 2026-09-18 
 The result remains the same as for the original query, but unrelated delivery rows are removed before the UNION ALL. The execution plan below shows how SAP HANA implements this reduction. 

 The filtered Region 2 order IDs are produced once by the DISTINCT operator and reused as a shared subplan. Each delivery table is then reduced through a HASH JOIN (SEMI): only delivery rows whose ORDER_ID occurs in selected_order_keys are passed to the UNION ALL. The resulting delivery rows form the right-hand input of the final HASH JOIN (LEFT OUTER). 
 The semi-joins reduce the delivery branches without producing NULL-extended order rows. Preserving unmatched orders remains the responsibility of the single LEFT OUTER JOIN above the UNION ALL. The plan therefore combines early reduction with the same result semantics as the original query. 
 The manual rewrite makes the reduction explicit by deriving the relevant order IDs and using them to restrict both delivery branches. 
 But is this manual rewrite always necessary, or can SAP HANA derive the same semi-join reduction automatically? 

 How SAP HANA can apply semi-join reduction automatically 
 The fact that the LEFT OUTER JOIN cannot be pushed down does not automatically imply poor performance. SAP HANA can introduce semi-join reduction as an optimizer transformation without changing the SQL statement. Whether it does so is cost based and depends on estimated cardinalities, internal cost evaluation rules, selectivity, table sizes, statistics, and the complexity of the execution plan resulting from the surrounding data model. 
 In the small teaching example used so far, the delivery tables contain only a few rows. Reducing them first offers little or no cost advantage, so SAP HANA may reasonably retain the original plan. 
 With larger data volumes, reducing rows before the UNION ALL can provide enough benefit for the optimizer to choose semi-join reduction automatically. The following example demonstrates this with large SAP tables. 
 Example with large SAP tables 

 Table 
 Description 
 Approximate number of rows 

 TADIR 
 Directory of ABAP Repository objects. It provides the object type, object name, and package assignment. 
 7 million 

 DD03L 
 Contains field information for ABAP Dictionary tables and structures. 
 15 million 

 DD03ND 
 Contains field information for structured Dictionary objects, including objects related to CDS data definitions. 
 2.5 million 
 Purpose of the query 
 The query selects the names and types of table definitions (TABL) and CDS data definitions (DDLS) assigned to package FINS_CODING_BLOCK in TADIR. It combines field information from DD03L and DD03ND with UNION ALL and left-joins the result to the selected repository objects. 
 The LEFT OUTER JOIN ensures that repository objects without matching field information are still returned. Objects with multiple fields produce one result row per field. with fields as (
 select d.tabname as objectname,
 d.fieldname
 from dd03l d

 union all

 select d.strucobjn as objectname,
 d.fieldname
 from dd03nd d
)
select t.object,
 t.obj_name,
 f.fieldname
 from tadir t
 left outer join fields f
 on f.objectname = t.obj_name
 where t.devclass = 'FINS_CODING_BLOCK'
 and t.object in ('TABL', 'DDLS');

title: Blog 10 - SAP ESM for HR - GoLive Cutover and the First 30 Days: Making It Stick
author: andreamazzanti
text:
The Final Mile 
 You have designed the organisation. You have built the service catalog. You have configured the channels, the routing rules, the SLAs, and the SuccessFactors integration. You have validated everything in UAT. The go/no-go criteria are green. 
 Now comes the part that determines whether months of careful work translate into a successful operation, or a painful first week that erodes stakeholder confidence before the system has had a chance to prove itself. 
 The go-live cutover is not the end of the implementation. It is the beginning of the HR operation. And the first 30 days after cutover set the trajectory for everything that follows. 
 This post covers both: the mechanics of a structured cutover, and the operational discipline of the hypercare period that follows. 
 What a Cutover Plan Actually Is 
 A cutover plan is not a project plan. It is a precise, sequenced checklist of every technical and operational action that must be completed in a specific order, within a specific time window, to transition from a configured and tested system to a live production environment. 
 The difference between a cutover plan and a to-do list is specificity. Every item has an owner, a start time, an end time, a dependency, and a validation step. If any item fails, the plan tells you what to do: who to escalate to, whether to pause and investigate, and what the rollback trigger is. 
 A well-built cutover plan for SAP ESM for HR typically spans 72 hours and is structured in three phases. 
 Phase 1 — Pre-Cutover (T-72 to T-24 Hours) 
 This phase is about preparation and final validation. Nothing changes in the production environment yet. The goal is to confirm that everything is ready to switch. 
 Key activities in this phase: 
 Configuration freeze 
 All configuration changes to the UAT and production environments are frozen. No new routing rules, no SLA adjustments, no catalog changes. What was tested in UAT is what goes live. Any change after the freeze requires formal change control approval. 
 Production environment readiness checks 
 Validate that the production ESM tenant is fully provisioned, that all SuccessFactors integration connections are active, that IAS and BTP configurations are in place, and that the email channel is pointing to the live HR mailbox (not the test mailbox). 
 Data readiness 
 Confirm that all HR agent user accounts are provisioned in production, IAS user groups are populated, and SuccessFactors permission roles are correctly assigned. Validate with a sample of five to ten employees across different countries that SSO works end-to-end in the production environment. 
 Communication preparation 
 Prepare all go-live communications: the employee announcement email, the HR agent briefing, the manager notification. Do not send yet, these go out in Phase 2. 
 Rollback plan confirmation 
 Define the exact trigger for a rollback decision: which P1 failure, within which timeframe, would cause you to revert to the previous HR service process. Confirm that the rollback procedure is documented, tested, and understood by the hypercare team. 
 Hypercare team briefing 
 The hypercare team, typically a small group of experienced consultants and HR SSC leads available full-time for the first two weeks, should be briefed, available, and clear on their escalation path before Phase 2 begins. 
 Phase 2 — The Cutover Window (T-24 to T-0 Hours) 
 This is the live switch. The production system goes live and the old process is retired. 
 Key activities in this phase: 
 Final production validation (T-24) 
 Run a final smoke test in production: create one case per configured channel, verify routing to each Agent Group, confirm SLA timers initialise correctly, validate SSO for one employee and one HR agent. This is not a full UAT rerun: it is a 30-minute sanity check that the production environment is behaving as expected. 
 Old channel retirement 
 If employees were previously emailing HR directly (individual inboxes, shared distribution lists), those inboxes must be redirected or decommissioned at go-live. Set up auto-replies on any retired HR mailboxes directing employees to the new HR portal or the new central HR mailbox. Leaving old channels open is the single fastest way to undermine self-service adoption. 
 Employee communications (T-4 hours) 
 Send the employee go-live announcement. The message should be short, clear, and action-oriented: here is your new HR portal link, here is what you do when you have an HR question from today, here is what happens if you email the old address. Avoid lengthy explanations of the system architecture. Employees do not need to understand how ESM works, they need to know where to go. 
 HR agent activation (T-1 hour) 
 Brief HR agents one final time. Confirm they can log in, see their queue, and access the knowledge base. Identify the hypercare contact for day one, the person they call if something is not working. 
 Go/no-go confirmation (T-0) 
 The project sponsor, HR SSC lead, and IT lead confirm go-live. Document the decision with a timestamp. The system is now live. 
 Phase 3 — Day One (T+0 to T+24 Hours) 
 The first day of live operations is the most intensive day of the entire programme. Plan for it accordingly. 
 What to monitor on day one: 

 Metric 
 What you are watching for 

 Case volume by channel 
 Is the self-service portal being used? Is email volume higher than expected? 

 Routing accuracy 
 Are any cases landing in the wrong queue? 

 SLA timer initialisation 
 Are all cases picking up the correct SLA? 

 Integration errors 
 Are any SuccessFactors lookups failing? 

 SSO failures 
 Are any users unable to log in? 

 HR agent queue depth 
 Is any team's queue growing faster than agents can handle? 

 Joule deflection rate 
 Are employee questions being answered without creating cases? 
 The hypercare team should have a live monitoring view open throughout day one. Set a check-in cadence, every two hours is appropriate, with a defined escalation path for any issue that cannot be resolved within 30 minutes. 
 What to communicate on day one: 
 If any issue affects a significant number of users, communicate proactively. Do not wait for the volume of complaints to force a response. A short message: "We are aware of an issue with X and are working to resolve it by Y", is far better than silence. 
 The 30-Day Hypercare Period 
 The hypercare period is not just about fixing problems. It is about stabilising the operation, tuning the configuration based on real usage data, and building the habits and disciplines that will sustain the system long term. 
 What to do in the first 30 days: 
 Week 1 — Stabilise 
 Focus entirely on resolving P1 and P2 issues. Track every defect, every workaround, every agent question. Daily hypercare check-ins. The goal is a fully stable system by the end of Week 1. 
 Week 2 — Tune 
 Review the first week's case data. Are routing rules working as designed? Are SLA targets realistic based on actual case complexity and volume? Is the knowledge base deflecting queries, or are employees finding it and not finding answers? Make targeted adjustments, but log every change. You need to know what you changed, when, and why. 
 Week 3 — Optimise the knowledge base 
 The first two weeks of live data will tell you which HR queries are generating the most cases. These are your highest-priority knowledge base gaps. Write or improve the articles for the top ten query types. This is the fastest way to drive deflection rate improvement. 
 Week 4 — First performance review 
 Run the first formal performance review with the HR SSC leadership. Present case volume, channel mix, routing accuracy, SLA adherence, and deflection rate. Compare actuals against the targets you set during design. Identify the three most important improvement actions for Month 2. 
 The Metrics That Tell You If It Is Working 
 By the end of 30 days, you should be tracking five key metrics regularly. By 90 days, you should have enough data to assess whether the implementation is delivering the outcomes it was designed for. 
 Self-service adoption rate 
 The percentage of all HR contacts initiated through the self-service portal. Target: >60%. If this is below 40% at 30 days, the employee communication and adoption plan needs attention, the system is working, but employees are not using it. 
 Tier 0 deflection rate 
 The percentage of employee visits to the self-service portal that are resolved without a case being created, answered by the knowledge base, or by Joule. Target: 30–40%. If this is below 15%, the knowledge base coverage is insufficient and needs immediate attention. 
 Joule deflection rate 
 If Joule is active: the percentage of Joule conversations that resolve without creating a case. Target: 15–25%. Below 10% at 30 days suggests knowledge base coverage gaps that Joule is drawing on is insufficient. 
 Tier 1 first-contact resolution rate 
 The percentage of cases handled by Tier 1 that are resolved without escalation to Tier 2. Target: 50–60%. Consistently below 40% suggests either that the Tier 1 scope is misconfigured (taking on cases that should go directly to Tier 2) or that Tier 1 agents need additional training or knowledge base support. 
 SLA adherence rate 
 The percentage of cases resolved within their configured SLA. Target: ≥95%. Consistently below 90% in the first 30 days is a signal to review either SLA targets (were they realistic?) or team capacity (are agents under-resourced?). 
 Continuous Improvement: What Happens After Hypercare 
 Hypercare ends, but the improvement cycle does not. The most successful SAP ESM implementations treat the system as a living platform, not a completed project. 
 Knowledge base maintenance 
 Assign ownership of the knowledge base to a named HR operations role. Schedule a monthly review of the top twenty case categories: are articles up to date? Are there new categories generating cases that need articles? A stale knowledge base is the fastest way to erode deflection rates over time. 
 Service catalog evolution 
 As you collect data on actual case volumes and categories, you will find that your Wave 1 catalog was a good starting point but not a perfect one. Plan a catalog review at Month 3 and Month 6, add L3/L4 categories where volume and routing complexity justify it, retires categories that generate no cases. 
 Routing refinement 
 Review routing accuracy monthly for the first six months. Misrouted cases are easy to spot in the data — cases that are reassigned shortly after creation are a routing signal. Use this data to tune rules progressively. 
 Wave 2 planning 
 If your go-live was a pilot (2–3 countries, as recommended), the first 90 days of live operation give you the most valuable input for Wave 2 scoping: what to replicate exactly, what to adjust, and what to add. Start Wave 2 planning conversations at Day 60, not after hypercare ends. 
 Closing the Series: Ten Posts, One Journey 
 This is the tenth and final post in "Implementing SAP ESM for HR — A Practitioner's Guide from Zero to Go-Live." 
 When I started this series, the goal was simple: to give customers and partners who are beginning their SAP ESM for HR journey a structured, practitioner-grounded guide that takes them from zero knowledge to a confident go-live. Not a marketing document. Not a product brochure. A real guide, written by someone who has been through these implementations and wants to share what actually matters. 
 Here is what we covered: 

 Blog 
 Topic 

 1 
 What SAP ESM for HR is and why it exists 

 2 
 The architecture you must understand before you configure anything 

 3 
 Designing your HR Shared Service Organisation 

 4 
 Building your HR service catalog 

 5

title: ABAP to Full Stack: Making Sense of What’s Behind a Fiori App (OData, Class, Virtual Element)
author: deiamolina
text:
Hello! I’m Andréa Molina. After more than 20 years in SAP, the new SAP world left me completely lost, so I decided to share my experience and learn together. I’m moving from classic ABAP to the SAP full stack, one real project at a time, drama included. 
 From overwhelmed to curious, my journey had (and still has) a lot of bumps. You can check my other posts here. I hope you find understanding and empathy here, and maybe a few laughs. 
 If you’re in the same boat, this series is for you. In this post: I will share my experience creating a List Report (a Fiori floorplan) built on a CDS view exposed as OData V4, with a virtual element calculated by an ABAP class. Plus a plot twist in Step 5. 
 A bit of background 
 On my journey I always try to use case studies that are real and will add value to the business. The library and ice cream examples just give me more anxiety and make no sense to me. So this time I’m turning an existing query/infoset (SQ01/SQ02) into a Fiori app, to understand how much effort and time it would take. 
 So far I have worked with the Basic template and one CDS KPI app, and I knew there were more template options to explore. This time I thought the List Report Page would work best (well, not really, but let’s move forward for now... surprise at Step 5 of this blog). 
 Before we move on, read this if you are asking "What on earth is List Report Page and Basic Template?" 
 When you create a new app from a template, you can choose among a lot of frameworks. Each framework provides a set of prebuilt files, structure and more. 

 You can read more about FloorPlans here: https://www.sap.com/design-system/fiori-design-web/v1-136/page-types/floorplans/when-to-use-which-floorplan 
 The project 
 Transform an existing Query/InfoSet (SQ01/SQ02) into a Fiori application. 
 Does SAP Make This Easy? 
 In my research and studying I couldn't find a tool that automatically converts queries into Fiori applications. If you know of a better approach, please share it in the comments. I'd genuinely love to learn. 
 The Challenge 
 … because I have never done before this project 
 Create a CDS view that delivers the data exactly the way I want it to be displayed, with logic and not just selection from the database 
 Create an ABAP class that is called by the CDS 
 Understand how the ABAP class and the CDS work together 
 Create a KPI on top of the report list 
 The best way to learn: get your hands dirty! A simple learning exercise 
 I am suggesting here a very simple example of CDS, class and app: create a List Report Page based on a CDS. 
 The result should show all the Sales Orders created in the last 30 days and flag the ones created today. 
 Step 0: Eclipse 
 The way to create backend objects for apps is using the ABAP Development Tools (ADT) in Eclipse. If you are new here, check this tutorial to set up your Eclipse ADT: https://developers.sap.com/tutorials/abap-install-adt/ 
 Step 1: The CDS Views 
 To get familiar with frontend and backend (together, they make the full stack), here is what is what. 
 Backend: where the data comes from. 
 Frontend: the screen the user interacts with. This part of the development is the backend. 
 What is backend: Where the data comes from. Put in very simple words. it's the data that will populate the frontend. 
 The CDS will select from I_SalesOrder, and we will use a virtual element (calculated by an ABAP class) to flag the orders created today. It will only return the last 30 days, so we don't select hundreds of records. 🥴 
 Why I_SalesOrder and not VBAK? 
 If you grew up in ECC like I did, you might be asking: why not use VBAK? 
 Tables move, CDS adapts. Moving from ECC to S/4HANA changed a lot of tables. Take VBUK, where we used to read the order status. Its fields now live in VBAK, so every program that selected from VBUK needs to change. But a program reading the status through I_SalesOrder will keep working, because SAP updated the view and left the interface alone. That's the idea behind released CDS views: SAP can rearrange it, and your app doesn't notice. 
 Clean core. Clean core is the promise of updating the system faster and more often than before, allowing companies to use the new technologies instead of waiting years for a hard and difficult system upgrade. To do that, you need to use standard objects. If you have already migrated to S/4, you know what I am talking about needing to adapt the system considering all changes. Using CDS views instead of tables is one step in the clean core approach. 
 It already speaks Fiori. SAP does the hard work of the joins and associations, so you just use it the way you need, and it's all ready for the day you want an Object Page. 
 Yes, I know. It's not our language YET, we don't know those CDS names yet, and it's so easy to use a table we know. But remember when VBAK sounded just as weird as I_SalesOrder does now? It stuck because we used it every day. This will stick too, if we choose to start. 
 Now we have AI to help us speed up our knowledge and search for the right object to select from. But I always use AI as a co-worker and never as the builder and be sure you add on the prompt to use best practices and use Standard objects whenever possible 
 So let’s go for it! Creating the CDS on Eclipse… 

 CDS Code @AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED //Authorization is not required
@EndUserText.label: 'Demo for ABAP Class' //Just a text
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true //
define view entity ZC_DEMO
 as select from I_SalesOrder
{
 @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 10, importance: #HIGH }] //The field below will be the first (10) column on the report
 @UI.selectionField: [{ position: 10 }] //The field below will be on the app as a search field
 key SalesOrder,
 @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 20 }]
 SalesOrderType,
 @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 30 }]
 SalesOrganization,
 @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 40 }]
 @UI.selectionField: [{ position: 20 }]
 CreationDate,
 @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 50, label: 'Created Today' }]
 @ObjectModel.virtualElement: true //The field below will use an virtual Element
 @ObjectModel.virtualElementCalculatedBy: 'ABAP:ZCL_VIRT_DEMO' //This is the Class you use to calculate the field below
 cast( ' ' as abap.char(1) ) as CreatedToday
}
where CreationDate >= dats_add_days( $session.system_date, -30, 'NULL' ) //Just select the last 30 days 
 UI annotations: how the backend tells the frontend what to draw 
 The Fiori app doesn’t know anything about our fields. The annotations in the CDS are instructions that travel with the OData service, and Fiori elements reads them to build the screen. 
 In plain English: the CDS doesn’t only deliver the data, it also sends instructions to the screen the user interacts with: “Hey, look, here is what you show in the table and here is what you show in the filters.” 
 In our code: 
 @UI.lineItem : this field becomes a column in the report. 
 @UI.selectionField : this field becomes a filter in the filter bar at the top. 
 The position number sets the order: 10 comes first, then 20, and so on. 
 Note: I prefer using a Metadata Extension (a separate file that keeps the annotations out of the CDS view), but I really want to keep this very simple here. 
 Step 2: Create the Virtual Class 
 Note: I know we could get this logic using a CASE in the CDS, but the idea here is to show how to use the class in a very simple example that everybody understand 😉 
 This part here is important, so let's translate what this part of the code is saying: 

 "Hey CDS, this field will use a virtual element. The value will be calculated by an ABAP class called ZCL_VIRT_DEMO. If nothing is returned, the value is blank. The field will contain a value of 1 char (ABAP CHAR1) and will be exposed as CreatedToday. Nice. See you in the class!" 
 So now we need to create the virtual class. 

 The code CLASS zcl_virt_demo DEFINITION
 PUBLIC "Can be used by other objects
 FINAL "Cannot be inherited
 CREATE PUBLIC.
 PUBLIC SECTION.
 "This makes the class a calculator for virtual elements
 INTERFACES if_sadl_exit_calc_element_read.
ENDCLASS.
CLASS zcl_virt_demo IMPLEMENTATION.
 "STEP 1 - Runs FIRST, before the database read.
 "Which real fields do you need to calculate your virtual field?"
 METHOD if_sadl_exit_calc_element_read~get_calculation_info.
 "Only if the app really asked for CreatedToday (names come in UPPERCASE)
 IF line_exists( it_requested_calc_elements[ table_line = 'CREATEDTODAY' ] ).
 "Tell SADL to also read CreationDate from the database
 APPEND 'CREATIONDATE' TO et_requested_orig_elements.
 ENDIF.
 ENDMETHOD.
 "STEP 2 - Runs AFTER the database read, once per package of rows.
 "Here we fill the virtual field.
 METHOD if_sadl_exit_calc_element_read~calculate.
 "Table typed with the CDS view, so we can access fields by name
 DATA lt_orders TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF zc_demo WITH DEFAULT KEY.
 "Copy the generic data into our typed table
 lt_orders = CORRESPONDING #( it_original_data ).
 "Read the date once, outside the loop (no need to ask on every row)
 DATA(lv_today) = cl_abap_context_info=>get_system_date( ).
 LOOP AT lt_orders ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<order>).
 "Created today? Mark with 'X'
 IF <order>-creationdate = lv_today.
 <order>-createdtoday = 'X'.
 ENDIF.
 ENDLOOP.
 "Give the result back to SADL (same rows, same order)
 ct_calculated_data = CORRESPONDING #( lt_orders ).
 ENDMETHOD.
ENDCLASS. 
 How to debug it 
 Go to SE24 and search for the class you created. 

 Double-click the method you want to debug and create an EXTERNAL breakpoint. 

 Important 
 You can preview the data in Eclipse, right? Yes, but there the class will not be called, and the virtual element comes back blank. Don’t do what I did: I thought my class wasn’t working and spent a long time trying to understand why! Let me save you the trouble: to see the class running, you need to create the service definition, the service binding and the app. 
 Step 3: Service Definition and Service Binding 
 Service Definition - You tell the OData service (the object that selects the data) what you want to be displayed in the result. 

 The Code @EndUserText.label: 'Service Definition for ZC_DEMO'
define service ZUI_DEMO {
 expose ZC_DEMO;
} 
 Service Binding - You expose the service definition as an OData V4 UI service, so the app can consume your CDS data. 

 Activate 
 When it does not activate 
 Depending on the architecture of your system, you might not be able to publish your service in Eclipse. If this is your case and you are using V4, you need to go to tcode /n/IWFND/V4_ADMIN. 

 Search for your Service Binding, select it and publish it. 

 Go back to Eclipse and you will see that the binding is now published. 

 Step 4: Creating a List Report Page 

 Just leave the project attributes as they are and finish the project. 
 You will get a message like the one below: 

 When it finishes, you will get this message: 
 Open Folder means you will only get this project in BAS. 
 Add Project to Workspace means it will be added to your other projects in BAS. I always use this option. 

 Then you can preview the application by right clicking on webapp 

 The terminal will run and another tab will open with your app! Voilá! 

 Step 5 - Adding a UI5 element on top of the report 
 Until here things went smoothly, but I want to add a Radial Micro Chart on top of the report. So my first instinct was to look for the controller and the view, but there was no MVC… WHAT??????? 
 But first, what is MVC? 
 If you don't know what MVC means and you are an ABAPer, please read this blog post: Getting cozy with familiar ABAP terms on your new BTP neighborhood 
 It was a surprise to me, and then I thought: "Wait... does every template have completely different code and a completely different way of developing?" Gosh! 😅 (Actually, I said a bad word, but let's keep this blog civilized.)
